headline: Blues Won't Quit at Higgins — Bass Stacking on Mackerel at the River Mouths
subhead: Bluefish are chewing through peanut schools from Pine Point to Prouts Neck while stripers hold tight on bait, waiting on the moon and the first cool nights to trigger.
body_markdown:
Higgins Beach threw up another good one Tuesday morning — gulls stacked over a peanut bunker school just outside the second sandbar, blues in the 4-to-8 pound range busting bait so hard it looked like rain on flat water. That's been the story up and down this stretch for going on two weeks now, and we flagged it last week: warm water was going to keep the bluefish aggressive and spread out right through Labor Day, and that's exactly what's happening. Pine Point's had the same show on the morning tides, and Prouts Neck picked up a run of blues Thursday on a light southwest wind that pushed bait tight against the rocks.

The bass are a different animal right now. They're around — thick, even — but they're staged on mackerel and sand eels at the river mouths rather than committing to any real blitz pattern. Biddeford Pool is holding fish on the last two hours of the incoming, same as it always does this time of year, but the bite is more of a mackerel-school-and-pick than a wide-open feed. Water's sitting in that low-to-mid 60s range at the river mouths — Saco, Kennebunk — and that's textbook early fall staging. Bass push up on the flood to work the mackerel pods, then slide back out with the ebb into the deeper cuts off the Pool. It's not blitz behavior yet. It's setup behavior.

The moon builds toward full on the 6th and 7th, and that's the piece that should tighten this whole thing up. Bigger tides mean harder current, which means bait gets pinned instead of scattered, which is when Biddeford Pool stops being a pick and starts being the best hour in the state again. If you can only fish one tide this week, make it the incoming at the Pool the evening of the 6th or morning of the 7th — that's when the moon and the bait density are most likely to line up.

On the plugging side, this has been a Danny/darter week at night and a pencil popper/Polaris popper week at first light. The Pool's north side, working the current seam off the sandbar as it floods, has given up bass to 28 inches on black Danny surface swimmers fished slow with a wide wobble — don't rush the retrieve, let the current do the work and just keep tension. Prouts Neck on that southwest wind has been a bucktail-and-popper combo game: white bucktail with a curl-tail trailer worked off the rocks on the down-current side for the bass holding in the wash, then switch to a pencil popper for the bluefish running through on top. Cape Elizabeth's ledges have had sporadic bass activity on the outgoing, mostly smaller fish in the 20-to-26 inch range, taken on green mackerel-pattern SP minnows worked just under the surface.

Mackerel themselves have been thick enough at Wells Harbor and Ogunquit to jig up a bait supply in twenty minutes on small diamond jigs or a mackerel tree — worth doing before you head to the Pool or Pine Point, because live or fresh-dead mackerel fished on a fish-finder rig has been outproducing plugs for the bigger bass holding deeper in the current seams. If you want a shot at something over 30 inches, that's the play: live mackerel, light enough weight to let it swim naturally, fished on the last of the flood tight to structure.

Flounder are winding down fast — a few keeper-sized fish still coming out of Wells Harbor and the back channels at Ogunquit on bloodworms and sandworms fished on the bottom, but that bite is thinning by the day as the water starts its slow slide toward fall temperatures. Cod remain mostly a boat game well offshore this time of year and nothing worth detouring the surf report for.

Looking at the next few days: expect the southwest wind pattern to hold, which keeps Prouts Neck fishable and keeps bait pushed toward the beaches rather than blown offshore. That's good news for the bluefish, which should keep chewing through Labor Day week as the warm water keeps them aggressive — that part of the pattern isn't changing yet. The bigger question is whether the building moon and the first real overnight cooldown — forecasters are watching for the season's first legitimate cool front — start compressing those staged bass schools into the kind of tight, current-driven feeds that make Biddeford Pool's incoming the must-fish window of the whole Maine season. If the nights start dropping into the 50s over the next week, look for that shift to happen fast, and look for it to happen first at the river mouths before it ever shows up on the open beaches. Until then, work the tides, work the mackerel, and don't be surprised if the best fish of your trip comes on the last twenty minutes of a tide you almost gave up on.
